Week 3 Data Blitz. Sampling Error

Seongmin Park and Gareth Yu

October 16, 2026

Loading Packages

library(psych)

Reading the Data

filepath <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/craigenders/psych250a/main/data/Cancer.csv"
blitz <- read.csv(filepath, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

1. Standard Error of the Depression Mean

Your code:

sd(blitz$Depression)/sqrt(nrow(blitz))
[1] 0.6614158

Whether your calculation agrees with the descriptive statistics output, what the standard error quantifies, what a sampling distribution is, and how the standard error relates to that distribution:

Yes, our calculation agrees with the value in the descriptive statistics output. The standard error quantifies typical deviation of sample means from the true mean. A sampling distribution is a distribution of the sample statistics from repeated samples of a population that we would expect to get given a true mean and sample size. The standard error relates to the sampling distribution because it is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution.

2. Central Limit Theorem Predictions

What the central limit theorem predicts about the shape, center, and spread of the sampling distribution, and what you predict you will observe:

The central limit theorem predicts that the shape of the sampling distribution of sample means will be normally distributed, being symmetric and having a center at 16, which is the population mean. It predicts that the spread of the distribution will be 0.66 (the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size). We predict the same.

3. Audit of the Simulation Code

AI’s response:

High-level conceptual recipe

Specify the population and sampling conditions

The simulation begins by defining a theoretical population with a known mean (16) and standard deviation (11.44), along with a sample size of 299.
Statistical purpose: establish the "true" population values and the sample size so the simulation can study how accurately sample means estimate the population mean.

Create a reproducible audit sample

A single random sample of 299 observations is drawn from the population, and the random-number process is fixed so the same sample can be reproduced every time.
Statistical purpose: provide a concrete example of one sample that could be observed from the population and allow others to verify the results exactly.

Check the characteristics of one sample

The script calculates the sample's mean, standard deviation, skewness, and excess kurtosis.
Statistical purpose: confirm that an individual sample looks reasonably consistent with the assumed population and inspect its shape, center, and spread. This helps verify that the data-generating process is behaving as expected before running the large simulation.

Visualize the single sample

A histogram of the audit sample is produced, with summary statistics displayed in a legend.
Statistical purpose: provide a visual check of the distribution of observations in one sample and illustrate that any single sample contains random variation.

Generate a large number of repeated samples

The simulation repeatedly draws 100,000 independent samples of size 299 from the same population.
Statistical purpose: mimic the process of collecting the same study over and over under identical conditions.

Compute and store a sample mean from each sample

For every simulated sample, the mean is calculated and saved.
Statistical purpose: build the sampling distribution of the sample mean, which shows how sample means vary across repeated samples.

Construct the sampling distribution

The 100,000 sample means are displayed in a histogram using fixed axis limits and bin widths.
Statistical purpose: visualize the distribution of sample means and show how concentrated they are around the true population mean.

Summarize the sampling distribution numerically

The simulation reports:
the sample size (299),
the mean of the 100,000 sample means,
the standard deviation of the 100,000 sample means, and
the theoretical standard error, σ/n\sigma/\sqrt{n}.
Statistical purpose:
Verify that the average of the sample means is approximately equal to the population mean (demonstrating that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator).
Verify that the spread of the sampling distribution is approximately equal to the theoretical standard error.
Demonstrate sampling error: individual sample means vary from sample to sample, but the amount of variation follows the standard error formula.
What the simulation is intended to demonstrate

In plain language, the simulation shows that:

Individual samples differ because of random chance.
Each sample produces a slightly different sample mean.
When many sample means are collected, they form a sampling distribution centered near the true population mean.
The variability of those sample means is approximately equal to the standard error σ/n\sigma/\sqrt{n}.
With a relatively large sample size (299), the sample means should cluster fairly tightly around the true mean of 16.
Apparent issues to inspect

HTML line-break tags (<br>) appear throughout the code.

These are not valid standalone R statements. If they are literally present in the script file, they will generate errors. They may simply be artifacts from copying the code into a web page or document.

The "verification audit" is not actually auditing the population.

It evaluates only a single random sample. Large deviations of skewness, kurtosis, mean, or standard deviation from their population values could occur purely by chance, so the audit should not be overinterpreted.

Population parameters are assumed rather than empirically verified.

The simulation generates data from a normal distribution with the specified population mean and standard deviation, so agreement with theoretical results is largely built into the simulation design.

Minor terminology check.

The reported "SD of the sample means" is the empirical standard error obtained from the simulation, while "Standard error formula" is the theoretical standard error. The comparison is appropriate, but it is worth recognizing they are two different quantities that should be close rather than exactly identical.

Your explanation of the simulation’s goal and major steps:

The goal of the simulation is to repeated sample from a population with a given mean and standard deviation, compute sample means, and create a sampling distribution to find the standard error. First, you have to specify a population and sampling condition, which include a population mean, standard deviation, and sample size. Next, it checks and visualizes the characteristics of one sample. Then, it generates a large number of repeated samples, computing the sample mean for each sample, and creating a sampling distribution with histograms and reporting the statistics of the sampling distribution.

4. Running the Simulation

The simulation code is below. Run the chunk as it is written.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# SAMPLING ERROR SIMULATION
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

# SIMULATION INPUTS ----

pop_mean <- 16        # population mean
pop_sd <- 11.44       # population standard deviation
sample_N <- 299       # sample size

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# SIMULATION CODE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

# VERIFICATION AUDIT ----

# makes the results identical every time the script is run
set.seed(250)

# draw a single sample of scores from the population
mysample <- rnorm(n = sample_N, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)

# mean, standard deviation, skewness, and excess kurtosis of the sample
audit_mean <- mean(mysample)
audit_sd <- sd(mysample)
audit_skew <- mean((mysample - audit_mean)^3) / audit_sd^3
audit_kurt <- mean((mysample - audit_mean)^4) / audit_sd^4 - 3

# tallest bar in the audit histogram, used to leave room for the legend
audit_barheight <- max(hist(mysample, breaks = 25, plot = FALSE)$counts)

# graph the sample
hist(mysample, breaks = 25,
     ylim = c(0, audit_barheight * 1.35),
     main = paste('Verification Audit: One Sample of Size =', sample_N),
     xlab = 'Scores')

legend('topright', bty = 'n',
       legend = c(paste('Mean =', round(audit_mean, 3)),
                  paste('SD =', round(audit_sd, 3)),
                  paste('Skewness =', round(audit_skew, 3)),
                  paste('Excess kurtosis =', round(audit_kurt, 3))))

# DRAW 100,000 RANDOM SAMPLES ----

# create an empty vector to hold the 100,000 sample means
samplemeans <- rep(0, 100000)

# draw a sample, compute its mean, and store the mean; repeat 100,000 times
for(s in 1:100000){
  sampledata <- rnorm(n = sample_N, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  samplemeans[s] <- mean(sampledata)
}

# EXAMINE THE SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION ----

# horizontal axis half-width
plot_halfwidth <- 4

# histogram bin width, also held constant so the bars are comparable
bin_width <- 0.05

# vertical axis maximum, held constant so bar heights are comparable
plot_maxcount <- 6000

# graph the 100,000 sample means with fixed bin width and axis ranges so graphs are comparable
hist(samplemeans,
     breaks = seq(pop_mean - 50, pop_mean + 50, by = bin_width),
     xlim = c(pop_mean - plot_halfwidth, pop_mean + plot_halfwidth),
     ylim = c(0, plot_maxcount),
     main = 'Distribution of 100,000 Sample Means',
     xlab = 'Sample Means')

legend(x = pop_mean + plot_halfwidth, y = plot_maxcount, xjust = 1, yjust = 1, bty = 'n',
       legend = c(paste('N =', sample_N),
                  paste('Mean of the sample means =', round(mean(samplemeans), 3)),
                  paste('SD of the sample means =', round(sd(samplemeans), 3)),
                  paste('Standard error formula =', round(pop_sd / sqrt(sample_N), 3))))

Whether the sampling distribution is consistent with your predictions from Question 2, and how the standard deviation of the 100,000 sample means compares with the standard error from Question 1:

The sampling distribution is normally distributed with a mean at 16.002 and a standard deviation of 0.664, which is consistent with our predictions based on the central limit theorem. The standard deviation from the sampling distribution is approximately the same as the standard error that we calculated in Question 1.

5. How Unusual Is a Sample Mean of 14.85?

A sample mean of 14.85 from a random sample of 299 people is fairly unusual because the mean is more than 1.74 standard errors from the true mean of 16. The difference of the sample mean from the population mean is 1.15 and the standard error is only 0.66, meaning that the sample is further from the true mean than the typical sample. Graphically, a sample mean of 14.85 is located fairly far into the tail of the distribution with the bar height being about a third of the height of the peak.

7. Why the Population Mean Does Not Matter

The sampling distributions from Questions 4 and 6 have the same shape and standard error. The only difference is that the center of the distribution from Question 4 is 16.002 and the center of the distribution from Question 6 is 13.002.

The population mean does not matter when the goal is to estimate the expected amount of sampling error across many samples because the standard error does not rely on the population mean. This is seen in the equation for standard error, which only includes population standard deviation and sample size.

8. Prediction for a Less Variable Population

What should happen to the shape, center, and spread of the sampling distribution when the population standard deviation is reduced from 11.44 to 6:

We predict that the center of the distribution will remain the same. The spread of the sampling distribution will be reduced, leading to a skinnier shape of the distribution and lower standard error.

9. AI on Variability and Sampling Error

Your prompt:

PASTE YOUR PROMPT HERE

AI’s response:

Conceptually, sampling error comes from the fact that a sample is only a subset of the population. Some samples will contain more high scores than average, some more low scores than average, and their means will therefore differ from the true population mean.

The key idea is:

The more spread out the individual scores are, the more opportunity there is for a sample to be unusually high or unusually low.

When individual variability is large

Imagine a population with scores ranging widely, such as from 0 to 100.

Some samples may happen to include many high values.
Other samples may happen to include many low values.
Because the scores are far apart, these chance differences have a substantial effect on the sample mean.

As a result, the sample means from repeated samples are more spread out, producing larger sampling errors.

When individual variability is small

Now imagine a population in which nearly everyone scores between 48 and 52.

Any sample will contain values that are already close to one another.
Even if one sample has slightly more high scores than another, the differences are small.
Therefore, the sample means remain close to the population mean.

As a result, the sample means from repeated samples are less spread out, producing smaller sampling errors.

Visual analogy

Think of aiming at a target.

A population with low variability is like throwing darts that all land near the center. Different samples tend to give similar means.
A population with high variability is like throwing darts over a much larger area. Different samples can produce quite different means.

The average location may still be the same, but the spread around that location is much larger.

Connection to the standard error formula

Your simulation compares the observed spread of the sample means with:

SE=σnSE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}

where:

σ\sigma = population standard deviation (individual-score variability)
nn = sample size

This formula shows directly that:

Increasing σ\sigma increases the standard error.
Decreasing σ\sigma decreases the standard error.

So the variability of individual scores acts as the "raw material" from which sampling error is created. A population with greater dispersion generates more variable sample means, while a population with less dispersion generates more stable sample means. In other words, larger individual differences lead to larger sampling errors; smaller individual differences lead to smaller sampling errors.

Whether AI’s response supports or contradicts your prediction from Question 8:

AI’s response supports our prediction from Question 8.

Your comparison with the distribution from Question 4, whether your predictions were correct, and whether the standard error formula agrees with the standard deviation of the 100,000 sample means:

The new sampling distribution has a skinnier shape and reduced sampling error compared to the original distribution from Question 4, but they have the same center at 16. Our predictons about the sample, center, and spread were correct. The calculated standard error of 0.347 agrees with the standard deviation of the sample means of 0.348.
